`ensure_ascii` is a class attribute on `StandardJSONSupplier` (`src/quill/json/supplier.py:144`). It decides whether non-ASCII characters are written as `\uXXXX` escapes or as literal Unicode characters in the serialized JSON string.

**How it works**
- `StandardJSONSupplier` is the supplier that uses Python's built-in `json` library. It is a subclass of `JSONSupplier`.
- `ensure_ascii` defaults to `True`. Its docstring says it replaces non-ASCII characters with escape sequences, which "may be more compatible with some clients". It can be disabled "for better performance and size".
- `StandardJSONSupplier.dumps()` (line 166) fills in the default with `kwargs.assumefallback("ensure_ascii", self.ensure_ascii)`. This is the same pattern it uses for `default` and `sort_keys`. The value is then passed to `json.dumps(obj, **kwargs)`.
- A caller can override the attribute per call by passing `ensure_ascii=...` to `dumps`. Setting the attribute on the supplier changes the default for every call.
- `response()` (line 189) builds its output through `self.dumps(obj, **dump_args)`. The setting therefore also applies to HTTP JSON responses. `dump_args` only sets `indent` or `separators`, so it doesn't override `ensure_ascii`.
- `loads()` is unaffected. JSON parsing reads escaped and literal characters the same way.

**Effect on output**
- With `ensure_ascii = True`, the snowman character U+2603 is serialized as `"\u2603"`. That is a 6-character ASCII escape, so the output is pure ASCII.
- With `ensure_ascii = False`, the same character is serialized as the literal `"☃"`. This output is smaller, but the encoder must then encode it as UTF-8 when writing bytes.

**Tests**
- `tests/test_objtext.py:47-53` (`test_objtext_as_universal_text`) sets `app.json.ensure_ascii` to `True` and to `False`. It expects `'"\\u2603"'` and `'"\u2603"'` respectively.
- `tests/test_trialing.py:110-114` sets `app.json.ensure_ascii = False`. It then checks that `SurroundingsConstructor(app, json="\u20ac")` produces a body that decodes to the literal `"€"`.

**History**
- `CHANGES.rst` (around lines 153 and 286) records that the old `JSON_AS_ASCII` config key was moved to the `app.json` supplier attribute.

`_got_registered_once` is a class-level boolean on `Schematic`, defined at `src/quill/sansio/schematics.py:172` with a default of `False`. It stops a schematic from being changed after an application has already copied its contents. Without it, later changes would apply to some applications and not others.

**How the flag is set and checked**
- `Schematic.enroll()` (line 273) sets `self._got_registered_once = True` at line 320. That happens right after it puts the schematic into `app.schematics[name]` and before it builds the `SchematicSetupStatus` and runs the deferred functions.
- `Schematic._verify_configuration_completed(f_name)` (line 213) reads the flag. If it is `True`, it raises an `AssertionError`. The message says the setup method `'<f_name>'` can no longer be called on the schematic `'<name>'`. It explains that the schematic "has already been registered at least once, any changes will not be applied consistently". It also tells the user to finish all setup before registering.

**Why registration is the cut-off**
- `enroll()` replays the schematic's recorded state onto the application. That state includes the `deferred_functions` list that `record()` fills, the nested schematics from `enroll_plan()`, and the fixed-directory (static) link rule.
- Anything added after that point would miss an application that had already enrolled the schematic. It would only reach applications that enroll it later, so different applications would end up with different behaviour.
- The check runs on the schematic's setup methods. `record()` and `note_once_only()` are visible in this file. `enroll_plan()` is decorated with the same `@preparationmethod` decorator. `record()` is also what `note_once_only()` calls internally.
- `tests/test_elementary.py:1690` asserts the message text `"setup method 'attach_link_regulation'"` for this case.

**Related design points**
- The flag is separate from `first_registration`. `enroll()` computes `first_bp_registration` by checking whether the schematic is already in `app.schematics`. That value goes into `SchematicSetupStatus`, and `note_once_only()` uses it so a function runs only on the first registration in an application.
- `_got_registered_once` is a single flag on the schematic object. It does not track which application the schematic was registered on.
- The application class has the same mechanism. `src/quill/sansio/app.py:416` has a matching "setup method ... can no longer be called" error, and `docs/lifecycle.rst:45` shows the message.
- `CHANGES.rst:160` records that calling setup methods on schematics after registration became an error, where it had previously been only a warning.

Static asset serving is split between two components that share the same base class. Each component has its own copy of the serving view and the cache-TTL method, and both read the same config key.

**Shared base: `src/quill/sansio/skeleton.py`**
- The common base class (extended by both the app and the schematic) holds the static-folder state.
- `fixed_dir` (line 224) is a property that joins `root_path` with the configured static folder. It returns `None` if none is set.
- `owns_fixed_directory` (line 241) is `True` when `fixed_dir` is set.
- `fixed_address_route` (line 249) is the URL prefix. It is either configured or derived from the folder's basename.

**Main app: `src/quill/app.py`**
- The `Quill` constructor (around lines 262-279) checks `owns_fixed_directory`. If it is set, the constructor calls `attach_link_regulation(f"{fixed_address_route}/<path:filename>", terminus="static", host=static_host, view_func=...)`.
- The view function is a lambda that goes through a `weakref` to the app. This avoids a reference cycle between the app and its view function.
- `Quill.fetch_file_transfer_ttl(filename)` (line 281) reads `current_app.config["SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT"]`. It returns `None` if the value is `None`. It converts a `timedelta` to seconds, and otherwise returns the value as is.
- `Quill.dispatch_fixed_document(filename)` (line 308) raises `RuntimeError` if there is no fixed directory. Otherwise it calls `fetch_file_transfer_ttl` and then `dispatch_from_folder(self.fixed_dir, filename, max_age=max_age)`.

**Schematic: `src/quill/schematics.py` and `src/quill/sansio/schematics.py`**
- `Schematic` in `schematics.py` subclasses the sans-I/O `Schematic` from `sansio/schematics.py`.
- The sans-I/O `Schematic.enroll()` (line 323) registers the static route only if `owns_fixed_directory` is true. It calls `state.attach_link_regulation(..., view_func=self.dispatch_fixed_document, terminus="static")`. Registration is deferred until the schematic is enrolled on an app.
- `Schematic.fetch_file_transfer_ttl` (line 55) and `Schematic.dispatch_fixed_document` (line 82) match the app's versions. The docstrings say "this is a duplicate of the same method in the Quill class".
- The code comment in `dispatch_fixed_document` explains the duplication. The shared helper only calls `fetch_file_transfer_ttl` on the app, so the schematic computes `max_age` itself and passes it in.

**Consistent caching**
- Both the app and its schematics compute `max_age` from the same config key, `SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT`, using the same logic. They both pass the result to `dispatch_from_folder` in `src/quill/helpers.py`.
- The default is `None`, so browsers use conditional requests instead of a timed cache.
- Where no explicit `max_age` is passed, `_ready_dispatch_document_options` (`helpers.py:387`) falls back to `current_app.fetch_file_transfer_ttl`. Ordinary file sends therefore use the same setting.

**The dual inheritance separates nothing. It lets one exception be caught as either kind of error.** The class is `SurpriseCharsetFault` in `src/quill/diagnosticassistants.py:17`:

```python
class SurpriseCharsetFault(AssertionError, UnicodeError):
    """Raised in places where we want some better error reporting for
    unexpected unicode or binary data.
    """
```

**What the code shows**
- The class has an empty body, only a docstring. There is no custom `__init__`, no `__str__`, and no logic.
- A repo-wide grep finds no other reference to `SurpriseCharsetFault`. Nothing in `src/` or `tests/` raises or catches it. The premise that it is "raised in debug mode" comes from the docstring's intent and from how its sibling classes work. It is not visible in current call sites here.
- The docstring says only that it exists "where we want some better error reporting for unexpected unicode or binary data".

**What each base contributes**
- `AssertionError` matches the convention of the other classes in the same file. `FormPayloadPathForwarding` (line 50, a debug-mode-only error) and `TroubleshootUploadsMissingKey` (`KeyError` plus `AssertionError`, line 23) both use it. The file's debug-mode diagnostics are therefore marked as assertion-style failures. Ordinary handlers for a specific error type don't catch them by accident, and they are a signal that the developer has misused something.
- `UnicodeError` (the `ValueError` subclass) keeps the exception compatible with code that already catches encoding and decoding problems.
- Together, code catching either `UnicodeError` or `AssertionError` still catches it.

**What the code does not show**
- I found no layering rule such as "validation lives here, encoding lives there". `diagnosticassistants.py` is a single flat module of debug helpers. Its other exceptions use the same multiple-inheritance pattern for the same reason, so it is a compatibility and diagnostics pattern rather than a layer boundary.
- Whether an issue counts as a "validation failure" or an "encoding issue" is not decided by this class. Both categories are covered by the one type.

The test that matches is `test_schematic_having_subhost` in `tests/test_trialing.py:117-138`. It goes from configuration, to route registration, to request context creation, and then to a full request. Each step depends on the one before it.

**Dependency chain**

1. **App and configuration** (lines 118-120)
   - `quill.Quill(__name__, subdomain_matching=True)` turns on subdomain matching.
   - `app.config["SERVER_NAME"] = "example.com:1234"` and `app.config["APPLICATION_ROOT"] = "/foo"` supply the host and path root. Later steps read both.

2. **Test client** (line 121)
   - `app.test_caller()` (`src/quill/app.py:669`) creates the client. It is created before the routes, but it only sends requests at the end.

3. **Route registration** (lines 123-129)
   - `quill.Schematic("company", __name__, subdomain="xxx")` stores the subdomain on the schematic.
   - `@bp.route("/")` registers `index`, which returns `quill.request.url`.
   - `app.enroll_plan(bp)` enrolls the schematic. `Schematic.enroll()` in `src/quill/sansio/schematics.py` runs the deferred functions, so the route is attached to the app with the schematic's subdomain. This step needs `subdomain_matching` from step 1 for the `xxx` subdomain to take effect.

4. **Request context creation** (lines 131-135)
   - `app.test_call_scope("/", subdomain="xxx")` (`src/quill/app.py:1423`) builds an `InquiryScope`. It uses `SurroundingsConstructor` (`src/quill/testing.py:27`) to build the WSGI environ.
   - `SurroundingsConstructor.__init__` reads `SERVER_NAME` and `APPLICATION_ROOT` from the config. It prefixes the host with the subdomain, giving `xxx.example.com:1234`. It uses `PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME` for the scheme. The base URL becomes `http://xxx.example.com:1234/foo`. This is why the assertion `ctx.request.url == "http://xxx.example.com:1234/foo/"` depends on step 1.
   - `with ctx:` pushes the context. Routing then matches the request to the schematic's route. The assertion `ctx.request.schematic == bp.name` depends on the registration in step 3.

5. **Full request** (lines 137-138)
   - `client.get("/", subdomain="xxx")` sends a real request through the app. It builds the same environ, dispatches to `index`, and the response body equals the same URL string.

**Related tests**
- `test_hostprefix_elementary_support` (`tests/test_elementary.py:1754`) checks `app.route(..., subdomain="test")` through the client using explicit base URLs. It doesn't use `test_call_scope`.

Filters, tests and globals that a schematic registers for the whole app are written into the app's single shared Jinja environment when the schematic is enrolled. Every render then goes through that same environment. Context processors work differently: they are stored in the app's dict and applied on each render.

**1. One shared environment per app**
- `App.markup_engine_env` (`src/quill/sansio/app.py:470`) is a `cached_property`. The first access calls `build_layout_ecosystem()`, which is overridden in `src/quill/app.py:385`. That method builds the Jinja `Ecosystem` and adds `build_link_to`, `config`, `request`, `session` and `g` as globals.
- Because the property is cached, the app has exactly one environment, and everything below writes into it.

**2. Registration on the app**
- `App.attach_layout_sieve`, `attach_layout_check` and `attach_layout_universal` (`sansio/app.py` around lines 686, 738 and 776) write straight into `markup_engine_env.filters`, `.tests` and `.globals`. The `layout_sieve`, `layout_check` and `layout_universal` decorators call them.

**3. Registration from a schematic, applied at enrollment**
- The schematic methods `attach_program_layout_sieve`, `attach_program_layout_probe` and `attach_program_layout_universal` (`src/quill/sansio/schematics.py:461, 497, 535`) define an inner `register_template(state)`. It writes to `state.app.markup_engine_env.filters`, `.tests` or `.globals` under `name or f.__name__`.
- Each method passes that function to `note_once_only()`. That wraps it in `record()` and only runs it when `state.first_registration` is true. The function is stored in `deferred_functions`.
- `Schematic.enroll()` (line 273) builds a `SchematicSetupStatus`, which carries `state.app`. It then calls every deferred function with that state (lines 334-335). This is the point where the schematic's filters, tests and globals reach the app's environment.
- The `program_*` variants are app-wide. Nothing scopes them to the schematic's own templates.

**4. Context processors**
- `program_scope_processor` (line 584) appends to `app.template_context_processors[None]`, under the same `note_once_only` gate.
- Schematic-scoped processors are merged into the app's dict under the key `name` or `name.key` by `_combine_schematic_functions` (line 410).
- `App.refresh_layout_scope(context)` (`src/quill/app.py:506`) runs the `None` processors, plus those for each schematic in `request.schematics` when a request is active. It merges their results, and values you pass in explicitly take precedence.

**5. Rendering uses the shared environment**
- `draw_layout`, `draw_layout_text` and their streaming variants in `src/quill/layouting.py` (lines 138-218) call `app.markup_engine_env.get_or_select_template(...)` or `.from_string(...)`. `_render` (line 126) then calls `app.refresh_layout_scope(context)` before `template.render(context)`. `src/quill/helpers.py:308` also loads templates from `current_app.markup_engine_env`.

**Ordering constraint**
- Because the environment is cached, Jinja options must be set before the first access.
- The schematic must be enrolled before the templates that need its filters are rendered. After enrollment, `_verify_configuration_completed` (`sansio/schematics.py:213`) blocks further setup calls on that schematic, so the set of registered functions can't change afterwards.

`MockLocation.__fspath__` returns `self.path`, which is whatever value was passed to the constructor. It does no conversion or copying, so `os.fspath()` gets back the same object.

The class is `MockLocation` in `tests/test_aids.py:11-22`. Its docstring says it is a fake `PathLike` object that stands in for a `pathlib.Path` and refers to PEP 519.

```python
class MockLocation:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path

    def __fspath__(self):
        return self.path
```

- `__init__` stores the argument as `self.path`.
- `os.fspath(obj)` calls `type(obj).__fspath__(obj)`. For a `MockLocation` that returns `self.path`.
- `os.fspath()` accepts only `str` or `bytes` from `__fspath__`. If a test builds `MockLocation("/some/dir")`, it gets that string back. If a test passed a non-string, `os.fspath` would raise `TypeError`, because the return value is not validated in the class itself.
- `MockLocation` is a stand-in for `pathlib.Path`, so tests can check that code accepting `os.PathLike` works with any path-like object. I found no `FakePath` name in the tests, so `MockLocation` is the only such helper.

The test is `test_pinpoint_program_throws` in `tests/test_terminal_tool.py:199-219`. It parametrizes `(iname, aname)` and calls `find_program(iname, aname)` under `pytest.raises(MissingProgramFailure)`. Each parameter pair reaches a different failure branch in `src/quill/cli.py`, and every branch is converted into `MissingProgramFailure`, a subclass of `click.UsageError` (line 37). The test therefore has one assertion for eight different failures.

**The eight cases and where each fails in `find_program` (`cli.py:241`)**

| `iname` | `aname` | Failure path |
|---|---|---|
| `"notanapp.py"` | `None` | `__import__` raises `ImportError` directly. `tb_next` is empty, so the traceback is shallow and it raises `MissingProgramFailure("Could not import ...")` because `raise_if_not_found=True`. |
| `"cliapp/app"` | `None` | Not a valid module name, so it fails the same way as the row above. |
| `"cliapp.message.txt"` | `None` | Treated as a dotted module name and fails to import. |
| `"cliapp.loadfailureprogram"` | `None` | The module imports but raises `ImportError` inside itself. The traceback is deeper (`tb_next` is set), so it raises `MissingProgramFailure` with the traceback text. |
| `"cliapp.app"` | `"notanapp"` | The import works. `locate_program_by_text` then hits `getattr` and raises `AttributeError`, which it converts to `MissingProgramFailure`. |
| `"cliapp.manufacturer"` | `'build_program2("foo")'` | Too few arguments. `attr(*args, **kwargs)` raises `TypeError`, and `_invoked_with_bad_arguments` finds that the frame never entered the function. It raises `MissingProgramFailure`. |
| `"cliapp.manufacturer"` | `"build_program("` | `ast.parse` raises `SyntaxError`, which becomes `MissingProgramFailure`. |
| `"cliapp.manufacturer"` | `"without_program"` | The function returns something that isn't a `Quill`. The final `MissingProgramFailure` ("A valid Quill application was not obtained") is raised. |

**Why it fails consistently**
- **Exception translation.** The three failure sources (import errors, `AttributeError` and `SyntaxError`/`ValueError` from parsing, and `TypeError` from bad manufacturer arguments) are each caught and re-raised as `MissingProgramFailure`. Most use `from e` or `from None`. That includes the nested import error, which is only reported by including the traceback text in the message.
- **Traceback depth.** The `sys.exc_info()[2].tb_next` check in `find_program` tells an import that failed to find the module apart from an import that failed inside the module. In both cases `MissingProgramFailure` is raised when `raise_if_not_found=True`.
- **`TypeError` disambiguation.** `_invoked_with_bad_arguments` (line 94) walks the traceback and looks for the function's code object. If the frame is missing, the call failed. If it's present, the error came from inside the manufacturer, and the `TypeError` is re-raised unchanged. That distinction is why the `'build_program2("foo")'` case gives a clean failure. A `TypeError` from inside the manufacturer would not be wrapped.

**The suppressed-error variant**
- `test_pinpoint_program_mute_throw` (line 222) checks `raise_if_not_found=False`. A plain missing module returns `None`, but the nested `loadfailureprogram` import error still raises `MissingProgramFailure`. So the option only suppresses the shallow "not found" case, not real import errors inside a module.
